stances.claim: Labor Day's two perennial demands - increase minimum wage and abolish contractualization - multiplied and amplified beyond May 1, 2023.

Wages SHOULD be maximized as much as possible - but Congress should NOT legislate across-the-board increases, because 'knee-jerk' legislation contravenes the wisdom of depoliticizing wages through Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards (under RA 6727 with tripartite composition and region-sensitive public hearings - NCR P570 nonagricultural; BARMM P341; agricultural lower). 'A one-size-fits-all response is never wise or beneficial in the long term.'

CJ concurs with the Foundation for Economic Freedom that the pending bills 'do not take into consideration the varying local and industry conditions' - and beyond FEF's stand, the wage boards should be empowered to act speedily, because once-a-year adjustment makes them 'decadent relics.'

If Congress must respond, it should amend wage-board authority/duties/powers 'instead of directly interfering in a framework that has withstood the test of time and only needs to be empowered to meet new and unforeseen expansions in this AI age.'

Government - especially Congress - should also maximize government-employee pay: 'Why should the private sector carry solely the burden of easing the pains of our people?' The government should 'walk its talk' instead of 'muscling with its raw power.'

Economists' inflationary objection is rebuttable - per Inquirer chair Palabrica's 5/2/23 column, government's multibillion-yearly subsidy programs (P20.5B in 2023) have not triggered unexpected inflation. Inflationary effect of reasonable wage increases 'can be solved by our economists.'
stances.rhetorical_move: third-party-data citation (Palabrica column as empirical rebuttal)

stances.claim: Abolition of contractualization is 'good only for grandstanding' and 'stands no chance of success' because seasonal (harvest farmworkers) and project-oriented (masons, carpenters) jobs are legitimate. 'Even past president Rodrigo Duterte, despite his election braggadocio of abolishing contractualization, did not and simply could not fulfill his election promise.'
But the abuse via 'endo' or '5-5-5' - 5-month rehire cycles evading 6-month regularization - is 'an abhorrent and illegal circumvention of the law.'

Per CJ's prior columns (latest March 27, 2022), the PH Constitution, Congress, and SC have been more protective and promotive of labor than US counterparts. Conclusion: 'while legal contractualization cannot be abolished, it should be minimized only to what is truly legal and constitutional.'

The 'AI age' reference as the future expansion that wage boards must be empowered to meet.

The cross-jurisdiction comparison - PH 'more than the US Constitution, the US Congress, and the US Supreme Court' - preserved as one of CJ's recurring frames celebrating Philippine labor-law generosity.
The 'minimize not abolish' resolution - CJ's signature analytical move on contractualization.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks May 1 Labor Day by addressing the two perennial demands that 'multiplied and amplified' beyond May 1, 2023 - increase the minimum wage and abolish contractualization. The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards, delegated by Congress under Republic Act No. 6727, fix region-specific minimum wages through tripartite (government-employer-worker) public hearings - currently NCR P570 (nonagricultural), BARMM P341 (lowest), with agricultural workers 'getting even less,' while Senate and House bills propose nationwide increases of P150-P750/day. While agreeing that wages should be maximized as much as possible, Panganiban disagrees that Congress should legislate across-the-board increases - this 'knee-jerk' reaction contravenes the wisdom of depoliticizing wages and ignores varying regional economic and labor conditions, since 'a one-size-fits-all response is never wise or beneficial in the long term.' He concurs with the Foundation for Economic Freedom that the bills 'do not take into consideration the varying local and industry conditions,' and further argues the wage boards have been 'wickedly slow' in adjusting wages - restrictions like once-a-year adjustment make them 'decadent relics.' If Congress must respond, it should amend wage-board authority, duties, and powers rather than 'directly interfering in a framework that has withstood the test of time and only needs to be empowered to meet new and unforeseen expansions in this AI age.' Moreover, the government - especially Congress - 'should also look into its own backyard and maximize the pay of government employees': 'Why should the private sector carry solely the burden of easing the pains of our people?' The government should 'walk its talk' instead of 'muscling with its raw power.' As to the economists' inflationary objection, Inquirer chair Raul J. Palabrica's column (5/2/23) noted that the government's multibillion-yearly subsidy programs (P20.5 billion in 2023) have not triggered unexpected inflation - so reasonable wage increases' inflationary effect 'can be solved by our economists.' Abolition of contractualization, on the other hand, is 'good only for grandstanding' and 'stands no chance of success' because seasonal (harvest farmworkers) and project-oriented (masons, carpenters on a specific house) jobs are legitimate, and 'even past president Rodrigo Duterte, despite his election braggadocio of abolishing contractualization, did not and simply could not fulfill his election promise.' But the abuse via 'endo' or '5-5-5' - services ended after a 5-month probationary period and rehired in 'endless cycles of five months' to evade the 6-month regularization requirement - is 'an abhorrent and illegal circumvention of the law.' Per CJ's prior columns (latest March 27, 2022), the Philippine Constitution, Congress, and Supreme Court have been more protective and promotive of labor than the US Constitution, US Congress, and US Supreme Court. Conclusion: 'while legal contractualization cannot be abolished, it should be minimized only to what is truly legal and constitutional.'
